short: A loan the lender flags as an early warning because payments are overdue, though not yet long enough to make it a bad loan.
kid: When a friend forgets to give back your toy for a few days, you start to worry a little. You put a small sticker on your list to remember to check on it.
detail: A special mention account (SMA) is the RBI's early-warning label for a loan that is overdue but has not yet turned into a non-performing asset (NPA). Under the rules as of 2025, a term loan is SMA-0 when principal or interest is overdue by 1-30 days, SMA-1 at 31-60 days and SMA-2 at 61-90 days; past 90 days it becomes an NPA. For cash-credit and overdraft accounts, SMA-1 and SMA-2 track how long the balance stays above the limit. Banks report large SMA exposures to the RBI's CRILC database, and the 2019 prudential framework requires lenders to start reviewing a defaulted large borrower within 30 days. Analysts watch SMA-1 and SMA-2 books because they hint at next quarter's slippages. A common confusion: an SMA tag is a warning, not a default classification, and many SMA accounts recover.
example: Say a borrower's ₹40,000 monthly instalment on a home loan falls due on 1 June and stays unpaid. Twenty days later the loan is SMA-0, at 45 days overdue it is SMA-1, at 75 days it is SMA-2, and once it is more than 90 days overdue it becomes an NPA.

short: A bank's troubled loans: bad loans, loans whose terms were eased for struggling borrowers, and sometimes accounts that are badly overdue.
kid: Imagine you lent toys to five friends. One lost a toy, and another asked for more time to give one back. Those two toys are the ones you worry about.
detail: Stressed assets is an umbrella term, not a single regulatory category. In India it usually means gross non-performing assets (NPAs) plus restructured standard advances; some analysts also add written-off loans still under recovery, security receipts received from asset reconstruction companies, and SMA-2 accounts. Because definitions differ, always check what a report includes. The idea matters because NPAs alone can understate trouble: a bank can restructure or evergreen a weak loan and keep it out of the NPA count. India's 'twin balance sheet' problem of the 2010s, when over-borrowed companies and weakened banks dragged each other down, was tracked through stressed assets; the gross NPA ratio of Indian banks peaked above 11% in March 2018. Investors use the stressed book to judge future provisions, profits and capital needs. The common confusion is to equate stressed assets with NPAs; the stressed figure is always broader.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has loans of ₹1,00,000 crore, gross NPAs of ₹5,000 crore and restructured standard loans of ₹2,000 crore. Its stressed assets are ₹7,000 crore, or 7% of loans, though its headline gross NPA ratio is only 5%. Adding ₹1,000 crore of SMA-2 accounts would take the stressed ratio to 8%.
formula: Stressed assets (common Indian usage) = Gross NPAs + Restructured standard advances

short: Loans that turned into bad loans during a given period, a measure of how much new trouble entered a bank's loan book.
kid: Your basket of apples was mostly fine last week. This week, three more apples went bad. Counting the newly bad apples tells you how fast the basket is spoiling.
detail: Slippages, or fresh slippages, are standard loans newly classified as non-performing assets (NPAs) during a quarter or year. They are the inflow side of a bank's bad-loan account: closing gross NPAs equal opening gross NPAs plus slippages, minus recoveries, upgrades and write-offs. The slippage ratio scales this inflow, usually dividing slippages by standard advances at the start of the period and annualising quarterly figures. A falling gross NPA ratio can hide rising slippages if the bank is also writing off or selling bad loans, so analysts read both together. Banks often split slippages by segment, because a spike in, say, unsecured personal loans or microfinance can signal a turning credit cycle. Do not confuse this with slippage in trading, which means getting a worse price than expected on an order, or fiscal slippage, a government missing its deficit target.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank starts a quarter with standard advances of ₹2,00,000 crore and ₹1,500 crore of loans slip into NPA during it. Its quarterly slippage ratio is 0.75%, or 3.0% annualised (0.75% × 4). If it also recovers or upgrades ₹800 crore and writes off ₹700 crore, its gross NPAs end the quarter unchanged.
formula: Slippage ratio = Fresh slippages during the period / Standard advances at the start of the period (annualised for quarterly data)

short: Money a bank sets aside from its profits to cover loans it expects will not be fully repaid.
kid: If you lend your toy car to a friend who often breaks things, you might save a few sweets to buy a new car just in case. You get ready for the loss before it happens.
detail: Provisioning is the accounting charge a lender books when it expects some loans to go bad. The charge reduces profit in the income statement and builds a loan-loss reserve on the balance sheet that is netted against loans; when a loan is finally written off, it is charged against this reserve. Under the RBI's incurred-loss norms as of 2025, banks hold a small general provision on standard loans (0.4% for most) and rising specific provisions as an NPA ages, from 15% for secured substandard loans up to 100% for loss assets. The RBI has proposed moving banks to an expected credit loss framework from April 2027, under which provisions come earlier. Provisions matter because they are often the biggest swing factor in bank profits. The common confusion: a provision is not cash leaving the bank, and it is not the same as a write-off.
example: Say, hypothetically, ABC Bank has a ₹10 crore secured loan that turns substandard, needing a 15% provision under RBI norms as of 2025. It books a ₹1.5 crore provision, so a quarter's profit before provisions of ₹20 crore becomes ₹18.5 crore before tax.
formula: Closing loan-loss reserve = Opening reserve + Provisions charged in the period − Net write-offs

short: The share of a bank's bad loans that it has already set money aside to cover; higher means a bigger cushion against losses.
kid: If three of your toys might break and you have saved enough pocket money to replace two of them, you are mostly ready. The more you have saved, the less a breakage will hurt.
detail: The provision coverage ratio (PCR) measures how much of a bank's gross non-performing assets (NPAs) are already covered by provisions. A PCR of 75% means three-quarters of the bad-loan book has been expensed, so only the remaining quarter, the net NPA, could still hit future profits if nothing is recovered. Indian banks often report two versions: a plain PCR, and a higher PCR including technical write-offs, which adds loans removed from the books but still being pursued to both the top and bottom of the ratio. Higher coverage signals conservatism and lower future provisioning risk, though it also reflects how old the bad loans are, since provisions rise as NPAs age. In options, PCR also stands for the put-call ratio, so check the context. A common mistake is reading a high PCR as few bad loans; it says nothing about how big the NPA pile is.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has gross NPAs of ₹8,000 crore and has provided ₹6,000 crore against them. Its PCR is 75% and its net NPAs are ₹2,000 crore. If it also has ₹4,000 crore of fully provided technical write-offs, its PCR including write-offs is (6,000 + 4,000) / (8,000 + 4,000) = 83.3%.
formula: PCR = Provisions held against NPAs / Gross NPAs × 100

short: An accounting method that makes lenders set aside money for loan losses they expect in future, rather than waiting until loans actually go bad.
kid: Before a picnic, you look at the clouds and pack an umbrella in case it rains. You get ready for trouble you can see coming, not only after you are wet.
detail: Expected credit loss (ECL) is a forward-looking way to provide for loan losses, introduced by the IFRS 9 accounting standard from 2018 after the 2008 crisis showed that the older incurred-loss model recognised losses too little, too late. Each loan's ECL combines the chance the borrower defaults, the share lost if it does, and the amount exposed at that time. IFRS 9 uses three stages: performing loans carry 12-month ECL (Stage 1), loans whose credit risk has risen significantly carry lifetime ECL (Stage 2), and credit-impaired loans carry lifetime ECL (Stage 3). In India, larger NBFCs that follow Ind AS 109 already use ECL, while banks, as of 2025, still follow incurred-loss norms, with the RBI proposing a move to ECL from April 2027. The US uses CECL, which books lifetime losses from day one. Note: ECL is a probability-weighted estimate, not a forecast that a loan will default.
example: Say a lender has a ₹1 crore loan where the borrower has a 2% chance of defaulting in the next 12 months and the lender expects to lose 45% of the amount if it does. The 12-month ECL is ₹1 crore × 2% × 45% = ₹90,000, booked as a provision even though the borrower is paying on time.
formula: ECL = PD × LGD × EAD (probability of default × loss given default × exposure at default), discounted to present value

short: The money a lender sets aside for bad loans in a period, shown as a percentage of its average loans.
kid: If you lend cups from your lemonade stand to friends, a few never come back. Counting how many you lose out of every hundred you lend tells you how careful to be.
detail: Credit cost, called cost of risk in Europe, is the annualised loan-loss provision charge expressed as a share of average loans, usually in basis points. It turns the rupee value of provisions into a number that can be compared across lenders of different sizes and across years. It is a key driver of return on assets: a bank earning a 3.5% net interest margin cannot stay profitable if credit cost runs at 3%. Analysts track it every quarter against management guidance, and a sudden jump often marks the start of a bad-loan cycle, as with unsecured retail and microfinance loans in India in 2024-25. Lenders to riskier borrowers accept higher credit costs in exchange for higher interest rates. A common confusion: credit cost is not the interest a borrower pays, and because it reflects provisions, it can differ from actual write-offs in the same period.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has average loans of ₹4,00,000 crore and books ₹1,200 crore of loan-loss provisions in a quarter. Its quarterly credit cost is 0.30%, or 1.2% (120 basis points) annualised.
formula: Credit cost = Loan-loss provisions for the period / Average loans (annualised)

short: Removing a loan from a lender's books because it is unlikely to be repaid; the lender can still try to recover the money.
kid: If a friend borrowed your crayon and lost it, you cross it off your list of crayons. But if your friend finds it later, you are still happy to take it back.
detail: A write-off removes a loan from the asset side of a lender's balance sheet once it is judged largely unrecoverable. The loss is absorbed by provisions already made, and any shortfall hits profit. Write-offs reduce reported gross NPAs, which is why analysts read them alongside slippages. Indian banks distinguish a regular write-off from a technical or prudential write-off, where the loan is removed from the bank's head-office books for accounting purposes but stays open in the borrower's account. In both cases the borrower remains fully liable and recovery continues through courts, the IBC or SARFAESI; any money recovered later is booked as income. The biggest confusion, common in Indian political debate, is treating a write-off as a waiver: a waiver forgives the debt, while a write-off is an accounting step and the bank keeps chasing the borrower. Still, high write-offs with low recoveries mean real losses.
example: Say, hypothetically, ABC Bank has a ₹500 crore NPA that is already 100% provided. Writing it off cuts gross NPAs by ₹500 crore with no fresh hit to profit, since the reserve absorbs it. If the bank later recovers ₹100 crore through the borrower's insolvency process, that ₹100 crore is booked as income.

short: Changing a loan's terms, such as stretching the repayment period or cutting the rate, because the borrower cannot keep up with the original deal.
kid: If your friend promised to give back five marbles today but only has two, you might say: give me one each day instead. You still get all your marbles, just more slowly.
detail: Loan restructuring is a change in a loan's terms granted because the borrower is in financial difficulty: a longer tenure, a lower rate, a repayment holiday, conversion of some debt into equity, or a partial write-down. It can save a viable business, but it can also be used to hide bad loans. Under the RBI's 2019 prudential framework, restructuring a stressed account generally means downgrading it to NPA, except under specific RBI schemes; the forbearance that let restructured loans stay standard was withdrawn in April 2015. Special windows, such as the COVID-19 resolution frameworks of 2020 and 2021, allowed one-time restructuring without downgrade in exchange for extra provisions. Analysts track the restructured book because a share of it often slips into NPA later. A common confusion: a normal refinancing by a healthy borrower is not restructuring; the trigger is financial stress.
example: Say, hypothetically, ABC Ltd owes ₹100 crore, due as ₹20 crore a year for five years, but its cash flows have fallen. Lenders restructure the loan to eight years at ₹12.5 crore a year, cutting the yearly principal payment by ₹7.5 crore while the total principal owed stays ₹100 crore.

short: Lending fresh money to a struggling borrower so it can pay off old dues, making a bad loan look healthy on paper.
kid: Your friend owes you five sweets but has none. So you give your friend five new sweets, and your friend hands them right back. It looks like you were paid, but you are still missing five sweets.
detail: Evergreening is giving a stressed borrower new credit, directly or through a related company or intermediary, so it can pay overdue interest or principal and avoid being classified as a non-performing asset. The loan stays standard on paper, the bank avoids provisions and its profits look better, but the real exposure grows and the eventual loss is often larger. Indian regulators have repeatedly tightened rules against it: the RBI's 2015-16 asset quality review exposed stressed accounts kept standard this way, and in December 2023 the RBI barred banks and NBFCs from investing in alternative investment fund schemes that had invested in companies borrowing from them, a ban it replaced with investment caps in 2025. Evergreening is a red flag for investors because it makes reported NPAs and slippages unreliable. It differs from legitimate restructuring, which is disclosed and carries classification and provisioning consequences.
example: Say, hypothetically, ABC Ltd owes XYZ Bank ₹500 crore and cannot pay ₹50 crore of interest due. The bank lends ₹60 crore to a group company, which passes ₹50 crore to ABC to pay the interest. The account stays standard, but the bank's exposure to the group has risen to ₹560 crore.

short: A temporary pause on loan repayments allowed by a lender or regulator; interest usually keeps adding up during the pause.
kid: If you owe your sister a sweet every day but you are sick for a week, she might say: start again next week. You still owe the sweets, and maybe one extra for waiting.
detail: A loan moratorium is a period during which a borrower need not pay instalments (EMIs), or sometimes only principal, without being treated as a defaulter. It is a built-in feature of some products, such as education loans that start repayment after the course ends, and an emergency tool: in March 2020 the RBI let lenders offer a moratorium on term-loan instalments falling due between 1 March and 31 May 2020, later extended to 31 August 2020, because of COVID-19 lockdowns. A moratorium is relief on timing, not on the amount: interest normally keeps accruing and is added to the loan, so the total cost rises. Do not confuse this with a moratorium imposed on a bank itself, such as the RBI's March 2020 moratorium on Yes Bank, which capped how much depositors could withdraw while the bank was rescued.
example: Say you have a ₹30 lakh home loan at 9% a year and take a six-month moratorium. Roughly ₹1.35 lakh of interest builds up over the pause (₹30 lakh × 9% × 6/12, ignoring compounding), so you restart repayments owing about ₹31.35 lakh.

short: A deal in which a lender accepts a single lump-sum payment smaller than the full amount owed and closes the loan.
kid: Your friend owes you ten stickers but can only find six. You say: give me the six now and we are done. You lose four, but you stop waiting.
detail: A one-time settlement (OTS), or compromise settlement, is an agreement in which a lender accepts less than the full dues, usually a lump sum or a few quick instalments, and releases the borrower. Lenders agree when the settlement beats what they expect to recover through courts, insolvency proceedings or SARFAESI, net of time and legal costs. The amount given up is the haircut. Public sector banks run periodic OTS schemes for small farm and MSME loans, and the RBI's June 2023 framework let lenders settle even with wilful defaulters and fraud accounts under board-approved policies, a move that drew criticism. For borrowers the catch is the credit report: a settled loan is marked settled, not closed, which can hurt credit scores for years. A common confusion is treating an OTS as free forgiveness; the lender books a loss and the borrower's record carries the mark.
example: Say a borrower owes ₹50 lakh on a defaulted business loan, and the bank expects to recover only ₹25 lakh after two years in court. It accepts ₹30 lakh as a one-time settlement, taking a haircut of ₹20 lakh, or 40% of the dues.
formula: Haircut (%) = (Total dues − Settlement amount) / Total dues × 100

short: A regulator's deep inspection of banks' loan books to check whether bad loans are being recognised honestly and provided for properly.
kid: A teacher checks everyone's toy box to see which toys are really broken, not just which ones children say are broken. Then everyone knows the true count.
detail: An asset quality review (AQR) is a special supervisory exercise in which a regulator examines banks' loan books account by account to test whether reported NPAs and provisions are accurate. India's best-known AQR was run by the RBI in 2015-16 under Governor Raghuram Rajan: inspectors identified large stressed accounts that banks were carrying as standard, often through restructuring or evergreening, and told banks to classify them as NPAs. Reported bad loans jumped over the next two years; many public sector banks swung to losses and were later recapitalised by the government. The European Central Bank ran a similar review of about 130 banks in 2014 before taking over supervision. More broadly, asset quality means how healthy a lender's loans are, tracked through NPAs, slippages and stressed assets. A common confusion: an AQR does not create bad loans; it reveals ones already there.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank reports gross NPAs of ₹10,000 crore on loans of ₹2,00,000 crore, a 5% ratio. An AQR finds ₹6,000 crore of hidden bad loans, lifting gross NPAs to ₹16,000 crore, or 8%. At a 15% provision on the newly recognised NPAs, the bank needs an extra ₹900 crore of provisions.

short: A specialist firm that buys bad loans from banks at a discount and then tries to recover more than it paid.
kid: Imagine a toy fixer who buys broken toys cheaply from a shop. The fixer mends them and sells them, hoping to earn more than the little it paid.
detail: An asset reconstruction company (ARC) buys non-performing loans from banks and NBFCs, usually at a steep discount to the amount owed, and then recovers money by restructuring the debt, enforcing security, selling the business or taking it to insolvency. Indian ARCs are set up under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 and regulated by the RBI; the first, ARCIL, began operating in 2003. ARCs typically pay part of the price in cash and the rest in security receipts (SRs), which pay out only as recoveries come in, so the selling bank keeps much of the risk. Under the rules as of 2025, the ARC must itself hold a minimum share of the SRs, giving it skin in the game. Selling bad loans lets a bank clean up its balance sheet. A common confusion: a sale to an ARC is not a full recovery, and payouts on SRs have often fallen short.
example: Say, hypothetically, a bank sells a loan with ₹1,000 crore outstanding to an ARC for ₹300 crore, paid 15% in cash (₹45 crore) and 85% in security receipts (₹255 crore). If the bank had already provided ₹750 crore, leaving a net book value of ₹250 crore, the price is ₹50 crore above book value, but only ₹45 crore arrives as cash and the rest depends on future recoveries.

short: An entity set up to take over large volumes of bad loans from banks, so the banks can clean their books and lend again.
kid: When the toy box is full of broken toys, it is hard to find the good ones. So you move all the broken toys into a separate box, and the first box feels fresh again.
detail: A bad bank is a separate institution, often government-backed, that takes over impaired loans from many banks at once, concentrating recovery work in one place and leaving the original banks with cleaner balance sheets. Well-known examples include the US Resolution Trust Corporation (1989), Sweden's Securum (1992), Ireland's NAMA (2009) and Spain's SAREB (2012). India's version, announced in the Union Budget 2021-22, is the National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (NARCL), majority-owned by public sector banks. It buys large NPAs, typically paying 15% in cash and 85% in security receipts backed by a government guarantee of up to ₹30,600 crore, while a sister company, IDRCL, handles resolution. Supporters say a bad bank speeds up clean-ups; critics worry about overpaying for loans and moral hazard. A common confusion: despite the name, a bad bank does not take deposits or make new loans; it is a recovery vehicle.
example: Say, hypothetically, a group of banks moves a bad loan with ₹2,000 crore outstanding to a bad bank at an agreed value of ₹500 crore. Under a 15:85 structure like the one NARCL uses, the banks receive ₹75 crore in cash and ₹425 crore in security receipts, against a debt of ₹2,000 crore.

aliases: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act
short: An Indian law of 2002 that lets secured lenders seize and sell a defaulter's pledged assets without first going to court.
kid: If a friend borrows your bike and promises you their skateboard if they cannot pay you back, this rule lets you take the skateboard without waiting for a judge.
detail: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI) gives banks and eligible financial institutions a fast way to recover secured loans. Once an account is an NPA, the lender issues a demand notice under Section 13(2) giving the borrower 60 days to pay. If dues remain unpaid, under Section 13(4) the lender can take possession of the secured asset and sell it to recover what is owed; the borrower can appeal to a Debt Recovery Tribunal. The Act also laid the legal base for asset reconstruction companies, securitisation and the CERSAI registry of security interests. It does not cover agricultural land or very small loans, and NBFCs can use it only above size thresholds set by the government, as of 2025. A common confusion: SARFAESI enforces collateral, while the IBC resolves or liquidates the whole company.
example: Say a borrower defaults on a home loan and owes ₹42 lakh including interest and costs. After the 60-day notice expires unpaid, the bank takes possession and auctions the flat for ₹50 lakh. It keeps ₹42 lakh and must return the ₹8 lakh surplus to the borrower.

short: A bank's own capital compared with its loans and other assets adjusted for riskiness, showing how much loss it can absorb before depositors suffer.
kid: When you build a sandcastle, a strong wall around it keeps the waves out. The bigger the wall compared with the castle, the safer the castle is.
detail: The capital adequacy ratio, called CRAR in India, compares a bank's regulatory capital (Tier 1 plus Tier 2) with its risk-weighted assets, which scale each exposure by how risky it is. Capital is the owners' money that absorbs losses first, so a higher ratio means a bigger cushion for depositors. Under Basel III the global minimum total capital ratio is 8% of risk-weighted assets plus a 2.5% capital conservation buffer. The RBI is stricter: as of 2025, Indian banks need a CRAR of at least 9% plus the 2.5% buffer, or 11.5%, with add-ons for systemically important banks. Falling short triggers restrictions, including the RBI's prompt corrective action framework. A common confusion: CRAR is not capital divided by total assets; that simpler measure is the leverage ratio, and a bank stuffed with low-risk government bonds can show a high CRAR while still being highly leveraged.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has Tier 1 capital of ₹12,000 crore, Tier 2 capital of ₹3,000 crore and risk-weighted assets of ₹1,00,000 crore. Its CRAR is (12,000 + 3,000) / 1,00,000 = 15%, comfortably above the 11.5% the RBI required as of 2025.
formula: CRAR = (Tier 1 capital + Tier 2 capital) / Risk-weighted assets × 100

short: A bank's highest-quality capital, mainly shareholders' equity and retained profits, which can absorb losses while the bank keeps operating.
kid: Think of the pocket money you saved yourself and put into your lemonade stand. If a jug spills, that money pays for it, and the stand stays open.
detail: Tier 1 capital is a bank's core, going-concern capital: the money that absorbs losses while the bank keeps running. It has two parts. Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) is ordinary shares, share premium and retained earnings, minus deductions such as goodwill and certain deferred tax assets. Additional Tier 1 (AT1) is perpetual instruments, such as AT1 bonds, that can be written down or converted into equity if the bank's capital falls too low. Under Basel III, Tier 1 must be at least 6% of risk-weighted assets; the RBI's minimum, as of 2025, is 7% before buffers. A common confusion: AT1 bonds count as Tier 1 but are far riskier than ordinary bonds, as investors learned when Yes Bank's AT1 bonds were written off in 2020 and Credit Suisse's in 2023. For the strictest view of strength, look at CET1 alone.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has CET1 capital of ₹9,000 crore and AT1 bonds of ₹1,500 crore, so its Tier 1 capital is ₹10,500 crore. With risk-weighted assets of ₹1,00,000 crore, its Tier 1 ratio is 10.5%.
formula: Tier 1 capital = Common Equity Tier 1 + Additional Tier 1; Tier 1 ratio = Tier 1 capital / Risk-weighted assets × 100

short: A bank's second layer of capital, mostly long-term bonds that are repaid only after depositors, which absorbs losses mainly if the bank fails.
kid: If your lemonade stand has a big spill, the coins you put in yourself pay first. If that is not enough, a friend who agreed to wait at the back of the line helps cover the rest.
detail: Tier 2 capital is gone-concern capital: it absorbs losses mainly when a bank is failing, protecting depositors and senior creditors. It includes subordinated debt with an original maturity of at least five years, general provisions up to a cap (1.25% of credit risk-weighted assets under the standardised approach), and some revaluation reserves at a discount. Because a bond close to maturity gives less lasting support, its recognition is phased out over the final five years before it matures. Under Basel III, total capital must be at least 8% of risk-weighted assets and Tier 1 at least 6%, so Tier 2 can fill at most 2 percentage points of the minimum; in India the minimums are 9% and 7% as of 2025. A common confusion: Tier 2 bonds rank above equity and AT1 but below depositors, so they are riskier than bank deposits.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has Tier 1 capital of ₹10,500 crore and Tier 2 capital of ₹2,500 crore against risk-weighted assets of ₹1,00,000 crore. Tier 2 adds 2.5 percentage points, taking its CRAR from 10.5% to 13%.
formula: Total capital = Tier 1 capital + Tier 2 capital

short: The strongest layer of a bank's capital: money put in by shareholders plus profits kept in the business, minus items that cannot soak up losses.
kid: Imagine your lemonade stand. The coins you put in yourself and the coins you earned and kept are the safest cushion, because nobody can ask for them back.
detail: Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) is the highest-quality slice of a bank's regulatory capital. It consists of paid-up ordinary shares, share premium, retained earnings and other disclosed reserves, minus regulatory deductions such as goodwill and other intangibles, certain deferred tax assets and large investments in other financial firms. CET1 is permanent, has no repayment date and absorbs losses first, which is why the CET1 ratio (CET1 divided by risk-weighted assets) is the headline strength measure for banks worldwide and a common trigger level for AT1 bonds. Basel III sets a 4.5% minimum plus a 2.5% conservation buffer, for 7%; as of 2025 the RBI requires 5.5% plus the buffer, or 8%, with more for systemically important banks. A common confusion: CET1 is not the same as book equity; deductions can make it noticeably smaller, especially after acquisitions that create goodwill.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has shareholders' equity of ₹10,000 crore, of which ₹1,000 crore is goodwill and other intangibles that must be deducted. Its CET1 capital is ₹9,000 crore, and with risk-weighted assets of ₹1,00,000 crore its CET1 ratio is 9%, above the 8% the RBI required as of 2025.
formula: CET1 ratio = (Common equity + Retained earnings + Disclosed reserves − Regulatory deductions) / Risk-weighted assets × 100

short: A bank's assets adjusted for how risky each one is, used to decide how much of its own money it must keep as a cushion.
kid: Carrying a pillow is easy, but a glass jar needs extra care. So each thing gets a score for how careful you must be, and the risky things need more padding.
detail: Risk-weighted assets (RWA) are a bank's exposures multiplied by risk weights that reflect how likely they are to cause losses, plus charges for market risk and operational risk. Under the standardised approach, cash and domestic government bonds usually carry a 0% weight, unrated corporate loans 100%, and riskier exposures more. RWAs are the denominator of every Basel capital ratio, so a bank can lift its ratios by adding capital or by cutting or reshaping RWAs. Regulators also use risk weights as a policy tool: in November 2023 the RBI raised the weights on many unsecured consumer loans and on bank lending to NBFCs by 25 percentage points to cool rapid growth, partly reversing the move in 2025. A common confusion: RWA is not total assets; the ratio of the two, RWA density, shows how risky a balance sheet is.
example: Say, hypothetically, ABC Bank holds ₹100 crore of government bonds at a 0% weight, ₹200 crore of home loans at a 50% weight and ₹300 crore of corporate loans at 100%. Its credit RWA is 0 + 100 + 300 = ₹400 crore, even though its total assets are ₹600 crore.
formula: Credit RWA = Sum of (Exposure × Risk weight); Total RWA = Credit RWA + Market risk RWA + Operational risk RWA

short: An extra layer of top-quality capital banks must hold above the minimum; dipping into it limits dividends and bonuses rather than closing the bank.
kid: You keep a few extra sweets in a jar for rainy days. If you have to eat some of them, you stop sharing sweets with friends until the jar is full again.
detail: The capital conservation buffer (CCB) is a Basel III requirement that banks hold an extra 2.5% of risk-weighted assets in Common Equity Tier 1 above the regulatory minimum. It is meant to be used in bad times: a bank whose CET1 falls into the buffer zone is not in breach, but must retain a rising share of its earnings by restricting dividends, buybacks and bonuses until it rebuilds. In India the RBI phased the CCB in fully by October 2021; under the rules as of 2025, this takes the CET1 requirement to 8% and total CRAR to 11.5%. A related tool, the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB), is a separate add-on of 0-2.5% that regulators switch on when credit grows too fast and release in a downturn; the RBI's CCyB stood at zero as of 2025. A common confusion is treating the buffer as part of the hard minimum.
example: Under global Basel III rules a bank needs 4.5% CET1 plus the 2.5% buffer, or 7%. Say, hypothetically, ABC Bank's CET1 ratio drops to 6.0%: that falls in the band where it must retain 60% of earnings, so on $1 billion of profit it can pay out at most $400 million in dividends, buybacks and bonuses.
formula: Required CET1 ratio including buffer = Minimum CET1 ratio + 2.5% (Basel III: 4.5% + 2.5% = 7% of risk-weighted assets)

short: A rule requiring banks to hold enough easy-to-sell assets, like cash and government bonds, to survive 30 days of heavy withdrawals.
kid: Keep enough water bottles in your bag for a long, hot walk. Then even if many friends ask for a drink at once, you still have enough to get home.
detail: The liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), introduced under Basel III after the 2008 crisis, requires banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets (HQLA), such as cash, central bank reserves and government securities, to cover their total net cash outflows over a 30-day stress scenario. Outflows are estimated by applying run-off rates to each funding source: stable retail deposits are assumed to leave slowly, wholesale and uninsured corporate deposits faster. Inflows can offset at most 75% of outflows, and the minimum ratio is 100%. The RBI has required 100% since 2019 and, under rules finalised in 2025, from April 2026 adds extra run-off for retail deposits that can be withdrawn through internet and mobile banking, a lesson from Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 collapse, when depositors sought $42 billion in one day. A common confusion: LCR is about surviving a short cash squeeze, not solvency; a well-capitalised bank can still fail a run.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank holds ₹30,000 crore of HQLA and expects ₹40,000 crore of stressed outflows and ₹16,000 crore of inflows over 30 days. Inflows are below the 75% cap of ₹30,000 crore, so net outflows are ₹24,000 crore and its LCR is 30,000 / 24,000 = 125%.
formula: LCR = Stock of high-quality liquid assets / Total net cash outflows over the next 30 days × 100 (minimum 100%)

short: A rule requiring banks to fund their long-term loans and assets with sufficiently stable money, such as capital and sticky deposits, over a one-year horizon.
kid: When you build a tall tower of blocks, you put the biggest, steadiest blocks at the bottom. Then the tower does not wobble when someone bumps the table.
detail: The net stable funding ratio (NSFR) is the longer-term partner of the liquidity coverage ratio under Basel III. It compares available stable funding (ASF), the part of capital and liabilities expected to stay for at least a year, with required stable funding (RSF), the part of assets and off-balance-sheet exposures that need such funding. Each item gets a factor: capital counts fully as stable funding and stable retail deposits nearly so, while short-term wholesale borrowing counts little; on the asset side, cash needs almost no stable funding, while long-term loans need most of their value covered. The ratio must be at least 100%. The Basel standard took effect in 2018, and the RBI applied it to Indian banks from October 2021. NSFR discourages funding long-term assets with short-term money, the pattern behind Northern Rock's 2007 run. A common confusion: LCR covers a 30-day stress, NSFR a one-year funding structure.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank's capital and liabilities, weighted by their stability factors, give available stable funding of ₹90,000 crore, while its weighted assets need required stable funding of ₹80,000 crore. Its NSFR is 90,000 / 80,000 = 112.5%, above the 100% minimum.
formula: NSFR = Available stable funding / Required stable funding × 100 (minimum 100%)

short: How a lender lines up when its money comes in with when it must pay money out, and how both react to interest-rate changes.
kid: If you promise your friend a toy tomorrow but the toy you are waiting for arrives next week, you have a problem. Planning so toys come in before you must give them out keeps everyone happy.
detail: Asset-liability management (ALM) is the discipline of managing the mismatch between a lender's assets (loans, investments) and liabilities (deposits, borrowings) in timing and interest-rate sensitivity. Banks naturally borrow short and lend long, earning a spread but creating a maturity mismatch: if deposits leave or short-term funding dries up before long loans repay, the lender faces a cash crunch, and if liabilities reprice faster than assets when rates rise, margins shrink. ALM teams slot cash flows into time buckets, measure gaps, run stress tests and use tools such as interest rate swaps and liquidity buffers; Indian banks report structural liquidity statements to the RBI. Mismatches were central to the crises at IL&FS and DHFL in 2018-19, which funded long-term assets with short-term borrowing, and to Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 failure. A common confusion: some mismatch is normal for banks; the danger is an unmanaged one.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has ₹500 crore of liabilities and ₹300 crore of assets repricing within one year, a negative gap of ₹200 crore. If rates rise by 1 percentage point, its yearly interest cost on that gap rises by about ₹2 crore (₹200 crore × 1%), squeezing net interest income.
formula: Gap (per time bucket) = Assets maturing or repricing − Liabilities maturing or repricing; Change in net interest income ≈ Repricing gap × Change in interest rate

short: Bonds a bank intends to keep until they repay, recorded at cost rather than market price, so price swings do not hit reported profit.
kid: If you buy a toy you plan to keep forever, you do not care what other children would pay for it today. You only count what you paid.
detail: Banks sort their investments, mostly government bonds, into accounting buckets that decide how price changes show up. Held-to-maturity (HTM) securities are bonds the bank intends to hold until maturity; they are carried at amortised cost, so market swings do not touch profit or equity. Available-for-sale (AFS) securities are marked to market through a reserve in equity, and held-for-trading (HFT) securities through profit and loss. Under the RBI's framework effective April 2024, closer to IFRS 9, Indian banks use HTM, AFS and fair value through profit and loss (with HFT inside it), and the old cap on HTM holdings is gone. HTM shields earnings when yields rise, but losses become real if the bank must sell, as Silicon Valley Bank showed in 2023 with about $15 billion of unrealised HTM losses at end-2022. A common confusion: no mark-to-market does not mean no loss.
example: Say, hypothetically, ABC Bank buys ₹1,000 crore of 10-year government bonds at par, and yields rise so their market value falls to ₹920 crore. In HTM the bonds stay at about ₹1,000 crore on the books and profit is untouched; in AFS the ₹80 crore loss goes to a reserve in equity; in HFT the ₹80 crore loss hits the quarter's profit.

short: A regulator's set of automatic restrictions on a weak bank, triggered when its capital, bad loans or borrowing cross set danger lines.
kid: If a child keeps getting hurt on the big slide, a grown-up says: only the small slide for now. Once the child is steady again, the big slide is allowed back.
detail: Prompt corrective action (PCA) is a supervisory framework that forces early intervention in weakening banks before they fail. The idea comes from the US FDIC Improvement Act of 1991. The RBI's framework, revised with effect from January 2022, uses three indicators: capital (CRAR and CET1), asset quality (net NPA ratio) and leverage (Tier 1 leverage ratio). Breaching a risk threshold triggers mandatory actions, such as limits on dividends, branch expansion and management pay, and discretionary ones, such as curbs on lending to risky borrowers or a forced capital raise. In 2017-18, 11 public sector banks were placed under PCA, curbing their lending until they were recapitalised; the last of them, Central Bank of India, exited in 2022. The RBI has since extended similar frameworks to NBFCs and urban co-operative banks. A common confusion: PCA is not a licence cancellation or a moratorium; depositors can use the bank normally.
example: Say, hypothetically, XYZ Bank has risk-weighted assets of ₹50,000 crore and total capital of ₹5,500 crore, a CRAR of 11%. That is below the 11.5% level (minimum plus buffer) that marks the first PCA risk threshold under the RBI framework as of 2025, so it would face curbs such as a ban on paying dividends until its capital recovers.
